title: Trust in protection
hook: he writes that no one can harm the one the Lord protects (Zafarnama)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the coiled one remains: four sons lost, and still something stands. Your line was still standing. What ordinary thing did you do on purpose? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-four.

Who gets to say the word safe? A child in a warm house says it easily. A man who, tradition says, has lost his home and his four sons has every reason never to say it again. And yet in the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh writes confident lines about exactly that: being protected. He writes them to the emperor himself, whose armies had chased him. That's the strange thing to sit with today. Not a promise of safety from someone who has never been hurt, but from someone who has.
screen: `WHO GETS TO SAY SAFE?` → `WRITTEN AFTER EVERYTHING WAS LOST.` → `SENT TO THE EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: Paraphrased, the thought runs like this: what can an enemy do, when the Friend is kind? The One who protects is the Lord, and no one can harm the one the Lord protects. In the letter, the Friend is God. Sit with what that can and can't mean here. It can't mean nothing bad will ever happen. The man writing it has already lived through the worst. So protected must mean something else. Some readers hear it this way: what the emperor can reach is the body, the fort, the family's lives. What he cannot reach is the bond between the Guru and God, and the faith that made the Khalsa. That's what is held, and that's what no army can take. Notice, too, that the trust doesn't make him passive. The same letter argues, accuses, and keeps going. Trust in protection, in the Guru's life, sits right alongside action. It's the floor he stands on while he works, not a reason to stop working. And there's a turn in who he's speaking to. Telling the emperor, in effect, you cannot harm me is not a boast about armies. It's a statement about where real power lies. For the Guru, it lies with the Friend. Sikh prayer, too, asks Waheguru for protection. Read beside this letter, that prayer isn't asking for a life without loss. It's asking to be held through it.
screen: `WHAT CAN AN ENEMY DO?` · `NOT: NOTHING BAD WILL HAPPEN.` · `TRUST SITS RIGHT BESIDE ACTION.` · `WHERE REAL POWER LIES.` · then, large: `PROTECTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in trust. Settle, and breathe. Let your weight sink into whatever is holding you up: the chair, the floor, the bed. Notice that you didn't have to earn its support; it's just there. Bring to mind one worry you're carrying today. Don't solve it. Set it down next to you, where you can still see it. Then, for the rest of the sit, let yourself be held. If you pray, you can breathe the name Waheguru, and rest in it. If you don't, rest in the breath itself. The bell holds the time.
Trust in protection. In the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh writes that no enemy can harm the one the Lord protects, after he had already lost almost everything. Today's word.
Your line: protected. Today, when the worry you set down comes back, say the word to yourself once, and then do the next useful thing. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite prayers for protection in the evening, and the Zafarnama's lines on the Lord as protector are recalled in katha as a picture of trust that stands alongside action.

threaten him with your remaining army.
fork.reveal: the Guru writes that when the Friend is kind, the enemy can do nothing. a statement about where power lies, not about armies.

notes: The Zafarnama lines ('what can an enemy do, when the Friend is kind'; no one can harm the one the Lord protects) are paraphrased; please check the wording and placement in the letter.
The hook's summary of the Guru's losses (home, mother, four sons) relies on tradition already told on days 1232–1233; please confirm it is fair to say these came before the letter.
'Every Sikh evening prayer echoes the same thread' refers to Rehras/Kirtan Sohila and Ardas asking for protection; this is a general gloss, please confirm or soften.

Editor pass: removed the mother's death and 'writing from a long way off' from the hook (not in the cited letter; losses now framed as tradition), softened 'Sikhs often hear' to 'some readers', and cut the unsourced claim that he had hardly any army left. The earlier note about 'every Sikh evening prayer' no longer matches the voice, which only says Sikh prayer asks for protection.
